papers.title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
papers.abstract: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.

papers.title: Thin-film lithium niobate integrated photonics at 493 nm
papers.abstract: Visible and near-ultraviolet light underpins applications from biophotonics to quantum computing, which demand fast control of optical amplitude and phase. Integrated photonics offers scalable control, yet most visible-wavelength platforms lack gigahertz-scale modulation. We demonstrate a thin-film lithium niobate platform at 493 nm integrating grating couplers, beamsplitters, ring resonators, and modulators. Segmented traveling-wave modulators achieve a half-wave voltage--length product of 450 mV$\cdot$cm, $>$20 dB extinction, and bandwidth beyond 50 GHz. Ring resonators show $2.9 \pm 0.2$ dB/cm propagation loss and quantify the platform's photorefractive response. This enables agile visible beam delivery for trapped-ion systems, although photorefraction and substrate uniformity remain key challenges to scaling.

papers.title: Accurate predictions of properties of energetic materials with tabular foundation models
papers.abstract: We use TabPFN, a recently developed tabular foundation model, to predict three properties of energetic materials: impact sensitivity, decomposition temperature and crystal density. Without any hyperparameter tuning, TabPFN outperforms the best published models for all three properties. It also substantially outperforms a wide range of established machine-learning models, including tuned gradient boosting (XGBoost), random forests and Gaussian processes. This holds both when the models are given hand-crafted molecular descriptors and when they are given learned representations from Chemprop's message-passing neural network. In particular, for all three properties, TabPFN applied to Chemprop's own embedding is more accurate than Chemprop's predictions. TabPFN is also among the fastest models we consider, more than an order of magnitude faster than XGBoost. As TabPFN predicts the entire distribution of the target rather than just a single value, it offers built-in uncertainty quantification, which we compare with the empirical distributions of compounds with repeated measurements. Finally, we interpret the predictions using Shapley values, which rank the features by their importance.

papers.title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
papers.abstract: Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a $12$-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of $0.969$. The query consumes $3.51\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}$ of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of $4.38\,\mathrm{W}$ and a peak of $64.4\,\mathrm{W}$. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.

papers.title: Simulating closed- and open-system dynamics of Tavis--Cummings lattices on fault-tolerant quantum computers
papers.abstract: Tavis--Cummings lattices couple cavities containing several emitters and host polaritonic many-body dynamics whose real-time correlations are costly to compute classically in two dimensions, especially when unequal emitter relaxation or dephasing rates break permutation symmetry. We analyze logical resources for fault-tolerant closed- and open-system simulation of an atom-resolved lattice with $L$ cavities, $N$ emitters per cavity, and photon cutoff $n\_{\max}$, including target observable estimation. Building on ladder-operator block encoding, we construct circuits for photon hopping and local light--matter exchange and combine them to encode the lattice Hamiltonian. By updating source and destination photon occupations in place, the hopping circuit eliminates the auxiliary $L\lceil\log_2(n\_{\max}+1)\rceil$-qubit photon register used by two-register implementations. Across three uniform-coefficient examples with $16$ to $256$ cavities, the controlled walk uses $4.75$--$8.11%$ fewer Toffoli gates than the paired two-register implementation under matched shared preparation, precision, control, and workspace conventions. For closed systems, we implement real-time evolution with generalized quantum signal processing and bound the cost of estimating retarded cavity spectral functions. For open systems with photon loss, emitter relaxation, and dephasing, we use a sampled first-order dilation and bound the runs and timesteps needed to estimate transient photon statistics such as $g^{(2)}(0)$. With state-preparation and measurement costs explicit, these estimates provide a reference for assessing fault-tolerant light--matter lattice simulation costs.

papers.title: Improved Myelin Water Fraction Estimation and Uncertainty Mapping in Multicomponent T2 Relaxometry via NNLS Bootstrap Aggregation
papers.abstract: Estimating the myelin water fraction (MWF) from multicomponent T2 relaxometry requires solving an ill-conditioned inverse problem, making estimates sensitive to noise. Regularization can improve stability but may introduce bias. Conventional NNLS-based methods also provide point estimates without directly quantifying voxelwise variability. To address these limitations, we propose the non-negative least squares Bootstrap Barycenter (NNLS-BB), combining residual resampling with repeated NNLS reconstruction. We average spectra and derived parameters across bootstrap replicates and use their standard deviations to characterize sensitivity to signal perturbations. The method requires neither an explicit spectral regularization penalty nor a training dataset. NNLS-BB was evaluated on 40,000 simulated voxels with signal-to-noise ratios of 50-1000, against conventional NNLS, two regularized NNLS methods, and a model-informed machine-learning (MIML) method. Scan-rescan repeatability was assessed across 20 white-matter regions in two independent cohorts comprising 13 healthy participants. NNLS-BB achieved the lowest MWF mean absolute error and root mean squared error in all simulated noise regimes. Mean absolute error decreased by 36-41% relative to conventional NNLS, alongside lower error dispersion. Compared with Bayes-Reg-$D^{-1}$ and MIML, NNLS-BB achieved comparable dispersion but substantially lower bias, although MIML reconstructed the full spectrum more accurately. In vivo, NNLS-BB yielded the lowest regional scan-rescan dispersion and highest mean correlation in both cohorts. Bootstrap standard-deviation maps provided complementary information about parameter variability. These results support residual-bootstrap aggregation for improving MWF estimation while providing voxelwise variability maps from a single acquisition.

papers.title: Semiparametric Inference in Panel Data with Interactive and High-dimensional Confounding
papers.abstract: This paper develops inference for a low-dimensional treatment coefficient in partially linear panel models with high-dimensional observed covariates and latent interactive confounding. Flexible adjustment for observed covariates can leave correlated factor components in treatment and outcome residuals, invalidating standard double/debiased machine learning (DML). We propose Factor-Augmented DML (FA-DML), which estimates treatment-side and reduced-form factor spaces from first-stage residuals. The estimator combines a feasible double projection with three-fold, unit-level cross-fitting. The double projection controls interactions between the two estimated factor spaces. The separate folds eliminate same-training-unit pairings in the leading disturbance components of the factor-estimation errors. Under fixed factor ranks, pervasive factor signals, strict exogeneity, and joint asymptotics in the number of units N and periods T , FA-DML is first-order equivalent to an infeasible oracle, is asymptotically normal, and admits consistent variance estimation. In the baseline simulation design with strong interactive confounding, FA-DML confidence intervals have coverage close to the nominal level. Standard DML and a two-fold variant that estimates both factor spaces on the same units substantially undercover. In an application to U.S. states, FA-DML finds that a 10% increase in the real minimum wage is associated with a roughly 1.1% lower 50/10 wage ratio. The estimate is stable across control sets and first-stage learners.

papers.title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_θ(x)\propto\exp(-E_θ(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.

papers.title: MammothDP: Private Boosted Decision Trees Ready for Trusted Hardware and Leakage-free Hyperparameters
papers.abstract: Data spaces like the European Health Data Space (EHDS) require the protection of sensitive data in studies during the data's processing and the study's release alike. In this work, we investigate how to implement this mandate using established trusted execution environments (TEEs) and timing side-channel hardening to protect the processing even under a compromised server, and the state-of-the-art differential privacy (DP) notion to protect the release of studies on tabular data. This combined setup could seem to complete the picture, but in fact raises unexpected security challenges that we mitigate by introducing MammothDP: a significant milestone towards a holistic machine learning system based on the recent gradient boosted decision tree learner S-BDT that is provably DP if used within a privacy filter, timing side-channel hardened, and deployed on a TEE. To achieve a strong privacy-utility tradeoff, we introduce two novel components: an early stopping criterion that adaptively selects the number of trees without any privacy overhead, and an improved rollback protection that is no longer vulnerable under timing side-channel attacks.

papers.title: Neural network scaling and generalization for 3D strain fields in heterogeneous materials
papers.abstract: Computational homogenization and coupled multiscale simulations of heterogeneous materials require repeated solution of mechanical fields on Representative Volume Elements, which becomes prohibitively expensive for high-resolution three-dimensional microstructures. Machine-learning surrogates can accelerate these computations, yet most existing approaches predict fields for fixed macroscopic loadings and provide limited guidance on how to scale network architectures for high-resolution 3D tensor-field prediction. This work presents a U-Net surrogate trained to predict the full 36-component strain localization tensor field in voxelized concrete mesostructures at resolutions up to $256^3$. Training localization tensors are generated with an FFT-based linear elastic solver, and an extensive hyperparameter optimization is performed to derive scaling rules and an accuracy-speed trade-off analysis. The results show that only network width and depth need to be scaled with problem complexity, while several conventional U-Net design choices, such as doubling channels after downsampling, are suboptimal for this problem. The final neural network achieves a Mean Absolute Error of 1.118% on both the validation and the held-out test sets, and an inference speedup of approximately 8.7x over the FFT-based solver on an Nvidia H100 GPU. Generalization experiments reveal transfer across aggregate volume fractions and highlight the importance of training on diverse morphologies. To safeguard reliability, a Maximum Mean Discrepancy metric computed on internal feature maps is proposed for detecting out-of-distribution microstructures without costly reference computations.

papers.title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
papers.abstract: Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold $F=1/2$. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach $N^*=27$ and $N^*=24$ qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.

papers.title: Dynamical GKP codes
papers.abstract: Dynamical codes protect quantum information with sequences of measurements, generalizing the stabilizer formalism of static codes. However, the dynamical formalism has been developed exclusively for qubit systems. While Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes are promising candidates for quantum computing that encode qubits in the continuous phase space of oscillators, no dynamical formalism has been developed for them. In this work, we bridge this gap and introduce dynamical GKP codes, combining continuous-variable lattice encodings with time-dependent translation measurement dynamics. To obtain the update rules and the distance of a given measurement sequence, we first generalize GKP codes to subsystem GKP codes using scaled symplectic lattices. Building on this structure, we adapt the ancestry, detector, and benign-error machinery originally developed for dynamical qubit codes. From this construction, we obtain a general and efficient method to compute the syndrome and distance of a dynamical GKP code from a persistent stabilizer lattice and a bounded inference window. We illustrate the framework with the example of the two-mode square-hexagonal Floquet GKP code. This code has reduced measurement weight compared to both the square and hexagonal GKP codes, while combining their set of logical gates, resulting in easier implementation of the full single-qubit Clifford group. Finally, we show that measurements with irrational symplectic overlap, which have no analog in discrete qubit codes, reduce to destructive homodyne detection in the single-mode case. These results extend an important qubit-code tool to continuous-variable systems and identify a new bridge between discrete stabilizer measurements and continuous homodyne detection.

papers.title: From Bias to Positionality: A critical grammar for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Bias has become a default lens for understanding what machine learning systems do and how we should relate to them. Bias is at root a deviation from a standard; in decision making systems we can supply a standard from outside: a law, a protected attribute, a benchmark, a statistical property. However, even there, biased is often used as a shorthand, without stating what the position taken is - a silent ``relative to''. In a general use of language models, nothing supplies the standard: there is no decision to audit and no counterfactual output, so the shorthand fails. We argue that positionality -- the located, articulated, owned and contestable position from which anything is said -- is the better grammar for the question these models now force: who is speaking, from where? Against the vendors' answer of nowhere and the seductive possibility of everywhere, we argue that when a model is taken as-if speaking, it speaks from somewhere, and this means positionality can describe models, and the way they are believed beyond their warrant, even though they are not accountable speakers. A model's positionality is laminar -- laid down across corpus, tuning, system prompt, application and the live conversation. We separate three sets of factors: the positionality of a model's creators, the behaviour they intend for it, and the behaviour it enacts, and situate current work within this matrix. This lets us highlight what each stratum inherits from the one below, with ruptures and collapses where that inheritance is disavowed. We then return to where models speak from, and discuss the implications for how models are made, read and held accountable.

papers.title: BioXArena-Pro: a research-grade benchmark for autonomous biomedical machine learning agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly proposed as autonomous builders of biomedical models, but existing benchmarks are small, near saturation or open to leaked information. We present BioXArena-Pro, 64 research-level modelling tasks from eight biomedical domains, each rebuilt from a published study; most hold out whole biological units such as species or cohorts. Across 22 agent configurations, the best scores 55.1 of 100, and the scaffold matters almost as much as the model. We re-ran a published method for every task: where the published recipe applies unchanged, the best agent and the methods tie; on rebuilt tasks the methods trail by 8.2 points, suggesting that agents gain by adapting to new data. Pretrained models (including biological foundation models) matter where the strongest agent uses them: forbidding them decreases its score on those tasks by 9 points. Every task was audited in several AI-assisted rounds and a final human review.

papers.title: Gradient Inversion through Linear and Affine Subspace Constraints
papers.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a machine-learning model without directly sharing their local datasets. However, as prior works have shown, the gradients exchanged during training may reveal sensitive information about client data. Most existing attacks usually optimize dummy inputs to match the true client gradients (Gradient Inversion Attacks), while some attempt to reconstruct them based on the observation that aggregate gradients from a fully connected (FC) layer are a linear combination of its inputs. In this work, we extend this observation by showing that aggregate gradients from an FC layer with the correct scaling are actually an affine combination of its inputs. We evaluate a gradient inversion attack that leverages either known linear-subspace information or its affine-subspace counterpart at each FC layer to improve reconstruction accuracy. Our results show that subspace-based methods can substantially improve reconstruction quality over the chosen baselines in certain settings. We further demonstrate that moderate overestimation of the batch size can generally improve or preserve reconstruction quality, even when the true batch size is unknown. We additionally examine reconstruction under gradient perturbations introduced by a differential privacy (DP) mechanism, providing insight into the effectiveness of the considered formulations under noisy conditions.

papers.title: MEOW: Medical Open-World Interactive Segmentation
papers.abstract: In open-world recognition, machine learning models not only make predictions on unknown structures ("generalized open-set"), but also continually learn and improve from those predictions over time. Interactive segmentation, despite its access to user feedback, has so far remained confined to the open-set setting. In this work we introduce MEOW, the first framework that turns non-interactive segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners without updating learnable model parameters. MEOW combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation to accumulate knowledge and thereby improve future performance. Focusing on medical data, we show that MEOW consistently improves its own predictions on classes never seen during training, and transfers zero-shot to unfamiliar domains, including micro-CT data and other imaging modalities.

papers.title: The Case for AI-Enabled Gate Monitoring as Farm Security in the UK: A PRISMA-Guided Review of the Evidence on Rural Crime, Livestock Predation and Farm Access
papers.abstract: Farm security in the UK rests on thinner evidence than its cost suggests. We ran a PRISMA guided review: twelve searches of Web of Science and Scopus on 2nd -4th November 2026 returned 1,183 records (761 unique), and grey-literature and hand-searches added 35 assessed sources. We synthesised 96 database records and 24 grey sources narratively. UK peer-reviewed evidence is small (16 records), and the main UK survey of crime and farmer mental health has 80 responses. Cost estimates rest on insurer claims: NFU Mutual put UK rural crime at £41.5 million in 2025, with livestock theft up almost 30% to about £4.5 million and dog attacks on livestock costing £1.95 million. The Home Office states that agricultural crime cannot be separately identified in its central data. We found no independent evaluation of cameras, sensors, trackers or marking; light and sound deterrents lost effect within one to five months in a systematic review of anti-predator interventions; and no study examined how often farm gates are left open or what follows. Camera-trap AI papers report accuracy on ecological datasets, none at a farm gate in the records we found, and in one comparison machine learning detected 41% of wildlife against 81% for analysts. We argue, as an inference from these gaps and not as a demonstrated effect, that continuous gate-level AI-mediated monitoring, as implemented in Fieldmark AI, would be highly beneficial for UK farm security. It would create the farm-level, time-stamped record that no official source holds, verify events that periodic human checks miss, resolve whether foxes, dogs or people were responsible, and give every other security measure something to be tested against. No study has yet shown that it reduces loss, and we set out the evaluation needed to show it.

papers.title: Orchestr.AI: A Unified Workflow for Training and Benchmarking of Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Machine-learning force fields enable atomistic simulations at near-reference accuracy and substantially reduced computational cost, but their development remains fragmented across software frameworks with incompatible data formats, configuration schemes, dependencies, and execution procedures. Orchestr.AI addresses this limitation through a unified workflow that coordinates different MLIP software frameworks, referred to as engines, for data preparation, model training, fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment. A common YAML interface defines each experiment, while engine-specific environment profiles preserve compatible software stacks and avoid dependency conflicts. The platform currently supports five MLIP model architectures, namely SchNet, PaiNN, NequIP, Allegro, and MACE, through their corresponding software implementations, providing automated configuration mapping and standardized dataset handling across these frameworks. Benchmarks on the rMD17 and 3BPA datasets show that Orchestr.AI reproduces the expected performance trends while enabling controlled cross-engine comparisons. Repeated executions with fixed configurations and engine profiles produce highly consistent results, demonstrating practical workflow reproducibility. Beyond training, Orchestr.AI provides modular architectural interfaces that connect trained models to ASE-based simulations, batch inference, epistemic uncertainty estimation, calibration, and active-learning workflows. The platform therefore provides a reproducible and extensible infrastructure for developing, comparing, and deploying machine-learning interatomic potentials, which we validate here through cross-engine accuracy and repeatability benchmarks.

papers.title: Conformal Risk Control for QoT-Aware Lightpath Feasibility Under Technology-Driven Domain Shift
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML)-based regression models support operational decision-making in optical networks but typically expose only point predictions, which carry no statistically controlled information about their reliability. This paper proposes a post-hoc conformal risk control (CRC) framework that keeps a pretrained AI/ML regressor fixed, provides a finite-sample guarantee on uncertainty band miscoverage, and maps the band to operational decisions through policy rules. The guarantee applies to interval miscoverage, while decision-error rates are evaluated empirically. We instantiate the framework for quality of transmission (QoT)-aware lightpath (LP) feasibility assessment, in which a regressor predicts optical signal-to-noise ratio (OSNR) under domain shifts caused by fiber, amplifier, and switching upgrades. Feature shift contribution scores identify the LP features whose relation to QoT changes the most across a technology transition, and two policies translate the bands into feasibility decisions, allowing operators to tune the trade-off between conservatively rejecting or aggressively accepting LP realizations. Experiments on open space-division multiplexing (SDM) QoT datasets over the CONUS topology show that, for a target coverage of 90%, the uncertainty bands meet the target in all 170 trials spanning 17 domain shifts and ten calibration-test partitions, whereas a source-only quantile regression (QR) baseline meets it in none. Under severe shifts, the efficiency-oriented (EO) policy empirically improves zero-shot (ZS) feasibility-decision accuracy from about 85% to above 99%, approaching a transfer learning (TL) policy while avoiding retraining. The framework provides finite-sample control of uncertainty band miscoverage for regression-based optical network decision support, with potential applications beyond QoT-aware LP feasibility assessment.

papers.title: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Error mitigation stands between variational quantum algorithms and useful results on today's noisy hardware, yet in practice a mitigation method is usually chosen once, by hand, and applied unchanged for the life of an experiment. This is a poor fit for quantum machine learning (QML), where the circuit and the noise drift as training proceeds, so the best strategy in one regime is often wrong in another. We present a generalized form of Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), which treats the choice of mitigation technique as an online decision made from an algorithm's own feedback. A single contextual-bandit controller observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior, and selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization per step. Because it depends only on this shared feedback interface, the framework applies unchanged across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning. Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman $χ^{2}=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$; pairwise Wilcoxon $p<4\times10^{-6}$). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly $1.3\times10^{4}$ shots from three to eight qubits.

papers.title: Floquet first- and higher-order topological superconductors: A review
papers.abstract: The current developments in quantum technologies are deeply rooted in quantum computation, with Majorana fermions and their topological protection expected to play a central role. In this context, topological superconductors (TSCs) provide a promising platform for investigating Majorana modes and their potential applications in topological quantum computation. In dimensions $d > 1$, the spatial localization of topological Majorana modes can be controlled in higher-order topological superconductors (HOTSCs), extending beyond the conventional framework of first-order topological superconductors (FOTSCs). In this review, we systematically survey the diverse landscape of topological superconductivity, ranging from FOTSCs to third-order topological superconductors (TOTSCs), in which the spatial dimensionality of Majorana zero modes (MZMs) is progressively reduced. We demonstrate how periodic driving protocols enable Floquet engineering of all these phases, even when the corresponding undriven systems are topologically trivial. Furthermore, we investigate various driving schemes and explore the interplay among spin-orbit coupling, magnetic fields, magnetic impurities, and symmetry-breaking mass terms in realizing Floquet higher-order topological superconducting (FHOTSC) phases, characterized by appropriate topological invariants. We also provide an extensive discussion of topological invariants capable of distinguishing conventional MZMs from anomalous Majorana $pi$-modes, which emerge at two distinct quasienergies and have no static counterparts.

papers.title: Learning the Brownian Motion in Machine Learning for Parametric Parabolic PDEs: A Backward Quadrature Approach
papers.abstract: We propose a backward quadrature learning (BQL) method for solving high dimensional parametric semilinear parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs). To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to extend the applicability of BSDE-based stochastic numerical methods to this class of PDEs. Specifically, inspired by the approach of learning the random variables (LRV)~\cite{BeckerJentzenMullerWurstemberger2024}, BQL incorporates learnable quadrature for Brownian increments at each time level into the backward recursion of BSDEs, enabling more efficient layerwise approximation of local conditional expectations. Furthermore, BQL introduces a continuation surrogate to facilitate the transfer of value-function information from subsequent to preceding time levels, avoiding nested quadrature while controlling the propagation of local approximation errors. Our main theoretical contribution is the derivation of a global error bound that explicitly characterizes the decomposition of the total error, together with a proof of first-order mean-square convergence under suitable approximation and integrability assumptions. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate that BQL achieves competitive solution accuracy while substantially reducing the amortized computational cost per query. For the HJB benchmark across the tested dimensions, with $Q=7$ parameter queries, BQL achieves computational cost reductions of approximately 40-fold and 4-fold compared with P$^2$INN~[2] and FBSNN~[3], respectively.

papers.title: AI-Adaptive Virtual Reality for STEM: Engagement, Retention, and Learning Outcomes
papers.abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) presents a com pelling opportunity to transform STEM pedagogy; however, empirical evidence evaluating AI-driven adaptivity, objective engagement metrics, and long-term knowledge retention remains sparse. This paper proposes and evaluates an AI-adaptive VR based solar system learning module deployed on Meta Quest 2, wherein a machine learning model dynamically adjusts in structional difficulty based on real-time learner interaction logs including dwell time, gaze patterns, and response latency. A controlled between-subjects experiment was conducted involving 120 secondary school students (mean age 14.3 years) across three schools in India, randomly assigned to three conditions: AI adaptive VR, standard VR, and traditional classroom instruction. Engagement was measured objectively through eye-tracking fixation density and heart rate variability (HRV), alongside pre-test, immediate post-test, and delayed post-tests at one week and one month intervals. Statistical analyses encompassing paired t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) reveal that the AI-adaptive VR cohort demonstrated significantly higher knowledge improvement scores (mean gain = 38.4 vs. 31.2 vs. 10.7), superior one-month retention (p < 0.001), and measurably elevated engagement across all biometric indicators. SEM confirmed immersion as a significant mediator between adaptive instruction and knowledge acquisition (\b{eta} = 0.63, p < 0.001). Post-session self-directed learning exploration was recorded at 80% among AI-adaptive VR participants versus 40% in the traditional group. These findings establish an evidence based framework for deploying AI-adaptive immersive learning environments in resource-varied STEM educational contexts.

papers.title: Proximal point algorithm for interval valued optimization problems with application to lasso problem
papers.abstract: In this paper, we consider a class of unconstrained interval valued optimization problems and using a suitable scalarization technique, we formulate an associated scalarized optimization problem and establish the relationships between the optimal solution of the scalarized problem and the $LU$-nondominated solution of the considered optimization problem. Based on this framework, we propose a proximal point algorithm and derive the global convergence of the sequence generated by the proposed algorithm along with the sublinear and linear rate of convergence for convex and strongly convex cases, respectively. Finally, we provide suitable numerical experiments along with comparative analysis with an existing method and applicability of the proposed algorithm on an interval valued lasso regression problem, highlighting its potential in machine learning models with uncertain data.

papers.title: MouldIt: Data Efficiency of Multi-Task Temporal Representation Learning in Injection Moulding
papers.abstract: Smart industrial solutions that can address multiple tasks require models that understand the underlying processes. We examine representation learning for modeling the injection moulding process as an example of such solutions. We consider its data efficiency and multi-modal benefit compared to classical machine learning alternatives. To this end, we synthesize a process-informed dataset based on a real reference cycle of an Erlanger Träger part. We then introduce MouldIt, a temporal convolution and attention based variational autoencoder that reconstructs in-mould signals, while classifying parts as acceptable or as one of our synthetic failure modes. We evaluate MouldIt on two tasks, known-class classification and unknown-class detection, across nine dataset sizes in single-modal and multi-modal settings. We compare it with an accept-all baseline and the classical methods k-nearest neighbors, logistic regression, random forests, and principal component analysis, which we adapt to support both tasks. MouldIt outperforms classical methods across both tasks from 4000 cycles in the single-modal setting and from 2000 cycles in the multi-modal setting. It achieves part sorting losses of 6.0 $\pm$ 0.7% and 1.0 $\pm$ 0.3% in the single-modal and multi-modal settings respectively, ranking first across all baselines and a combination of principal component analysis and random forests.

papers.title: Min-CSPs on Complete Instances III: Nearly Optimal Characterizations of Approximation for Symmetric CSPs
papers.abstract: This paper studies complete Min-$k$-CSPs: an instance on $n$ variables has one nontrivial constraint for every $k$-set of variables (so $\binom{n}{k}$ constraints in total), and the goal is to find an assignment that minimizes the number of unsatisfied constraints. They are motivated by the connections to machine learning and data science, as well as the possibility of being testbeds for new algorithmic techniques. Previous recent results presented polynomial-time algorithms for the decision version of every complete Boolean $k$-CSP, which is a necessary condition for any multiplicative approximations for the minimization version, but nontrivial approximation results have been limited to fragile CSPs, 2-SAT, and NAE-3-SAT, leaving the approximability of most complete Boolean Min-CSPs open, including complete Min-$k$-SAT.   In this paper, we resolve this question, up to nearly matching factors, for the natural class of symmetric Boolean predicates. Given $A \subseteq \{0, \dots, k\}$, Min-CSP($A$) is a Min-$k$-CSP where each constraint is specified by $k$ literals and is satisfied if the number of true literals belongs to $A$. Let $w(A)$ be the maximum number of consecutive integers in $A$. Our main results for complete Min-CSP($A$) are (1) a QPTAS for $w(A) \leq 2$ and (2) an $\widetilde{O}(n^{w(A)-3})$-approximation for $w(A) \geq 3$, as well as almost matching hardness results for the latter. Our QPTAS for $w(A)=2$ significantly improves the previous $O(1)$-approximation for Min-2-SAT and the $\operatorname{polylog}(n)$-approximation for Min-NAE-3-SAT, as well as extends the PTAS for fragile CSPs (i.e., $w(A) = 1$).

papers.title: Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that combine accuracy, throughput, low latency, and scalability to large numbers of physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, erasures from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements are a dominant error mechanism, motivating decoders that remain accurate at high erasure rates. We introduce PRISM, a transformer-based machine-learning decoder designed to exploit the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. We benchmark PRISM across a wide range of fault-tolerant protocols based on surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes, with distances up to 24. Across these benchmarks, PRISM matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. We further optimize the decoder and its real-time hardware implementation to reduce latency while maintaining accuracy. Our optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA can decode logical blocks of distance 8 in both space and time, demonstrating a latency of 6.59 microseconds and an amortized decoding time of 1.56 microseconds per logical block is possible. These results show that machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

papers.title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Non-intrusive Model Reduction under Data Scarcity
papers.abstract: Many-query analyses, in which a computational model is repeatedly evaluated, play an important role in uncertainty quantification and optimization for engineering design. However, many-query analyses can be prohibitively expensive when considering high-fidelity numerical models, especially those governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). Surrogate modeling replaces costly simulations with cheap approximations, enabling practical uncertainty quantification and design workflows. Machine learning (ML) approaches to surrogate modeling have gained significant traction in the development of surrogate models due to their non-intrusive nature; they do not require access to the underlying simulation code. The Operator Inference (OpInf) approach, in particular, fits reduced operators to state and corresponding time derivative data. However, high-fidelity training data is scarce due to limited computational budgets, and OpInf models trained on such scarce data often exhibit high variance, a critical liability in high-risk engineering design. We propose Multifidelity Operator Inference (MF-OpInf), which reduces this variance by supplementing scarce high-fidelity snapshots with abundant low-fidelity data drawn from coarser discretizations of the same problem. MF-OpInf handles data across varying fidelity levels by utilizing a multifidelity linear regression framework to estimate the reduced operators. Numerical experiments on model PDE problems demonstrate that MF-OpInf predicts PDE solution fields with higher accuracy compared to the high-fidelity-only OpInf with the same computational budget.

papers.title: How anion composition governs structural frameworks and Li-ion transport in oxychloride solid-state electrolytes
papers.abstract: Mixed-anion lithium oxychlorides exhibit high Li conductivity, but the relationship between oxygen content, structural framework, and Li-ion transport remains unclear. Here, crystal structure prediction and molecular dynamics simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials are used to examine $\mathrm{Li}_yM\mathrm{O}_x\mathrm{Cl}_{6-2x}$ ($M$ = Nb and Ta [Group 5] and $M$ = Ti, Zr, and Hf [Group 4]). Increasing oxygen content changes isolated chloride-rich polyhedra into one-dimensional chains and subsequently more highly connected two- and three-dimensional frameworks. In the Group 5 series, fast Li diffusion occurs over $x \approx 0.67$--1.5, where the Li sites form a three-dimensional percolating network. Potential of mean force maps and nudged elastic band calculations reveal that fast Li-ion transport requires a low-dimensional framework supporting long-range migration through undercoordinated Li sites with low barriers, together with similar energies across Li sites. Finally, we perform fine-grid compositional search, which identifies $\mathrm{LiNbO}_{0.67}\mathrm{Cl}_{4.67}$, $\mathrm{LiTaO}_{0.75}\mathrm{Cl}_{4.5}$, $\mathrm{LiNbO}_{1.5}\mathrm{Cl}_3$, and $\mathrm{LiTaO}_{1.5}\mathrm{Cl}_3$ as stable candidates with predicted room-temperature self-diffusivities of up to $\sim 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}^2/\mathrm{s}$. These findings establish how oxygen content controls framework and Li-ion transport, guiding the design of lithium oxyhalide electrolytes.

papers.title: Distribution Shift Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery using Machine Learning Models
papers.abstract: Remote sensing imagery acquired by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) supports wide range of applications; however, deploying machine learning (ML) models on resource-constrained aerial platforms introduces challenges beyond predictive accuracy, particularly when deployment data differ from the distributions observed during training. Such shifts are common in remote sensing due to geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual variations. A practical solution is to equip deployed models with mechanisms that detect emerging distribution shifts and support subsequent responsive actions. This paper presents an empirical case study of three open-source detection tools: (i) Alibi-Detect; (ii) NannyML; and (iii) PyTorch-OOD. Using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts, we evaluate both detection effectiveness and computational latency of these tools. Our results reveal differences in detection behavior and processing cost across methods and implementations, highlighting trade-offs between detection capability and response-time. These findings motivate further work toward lightweight, and latency-aware monitoring mechanisms for resource-constrained systems.

papers.title: You Don't Need Feature Learning to Do In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: How should we understand memorization vs. generalization in in-context learning (ICL) tasks, and when does one happen vs. the other? To investigate, we study how rotation-invariant kernel machines learn the ICL linear regression task proposed by Raventos et al. (2023). By decomposing the task in the kernel eigenbasis, we obtain a spectral picture of learning in this ICL setting. This picture reveals that as sample size grows, kernel machines learn successively-higher-degree components of the memorizing solution, which depend upon successively-higher-degree statistics of the training task set. The generalizing solution is approximately a low-degree truncation of the memorizing solution, and so the model first generalizes, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds.   The takeaways are threefold. First, if this case is indicative, learning a "generalizing" solution on an ICL task is really just underfitting the memorizing solution! Second, the fact that kernel machines can generalize on this task means that feature learning is inessential to ICL. Third, transformers empirically trained to do ICL are shown to memorize tasks through the higher-order statistics of the training tasks that the kernel-based theory predicts, suggesting it applies even to models capable of feature learning.

papers.title: Designing Accessible and Rigorous ML Experiments: No-Code Visual Workflows and Structured Guidance for Beginners
papers.abstract: Designing machine learning (ML) experiments requires beginners to plan a methodologically sound workflow and implement it in a concrete environment. We evaluated two forms of support in two within-participant studies with 18 predominantly technically trained participants: mlguide, which provides structured, evidence- backed guidance for workflow design, and AI Sandbox, a visual no-code environment for workflow implementation. After using mlguide, participants produced better high-level workflow designs, but their scores on a quiz about specific methodological choices did not improve significantly. Compared with Google Colab, AI Sandbox received higher hedonic user experience ratings, while perceived workload and acceptance did not differ significantly. These findings suggest that different forms of interactive support help with differ- ent aspects of beginner ML experimentation. The paper contributes a reusable evaluation task with instructions, a modified dataset, and a quiz, as well as empirical evidence on structured guidance for workflow design and on the experience of implementing workflows in visual and notebook-based environments.

papers.title: Reconstructing Boundary Layer Wind Profiles with Machine Learning: A Comparative Study on IGRA Radiosonde Data
papers.abstract: Wind profiles in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) drive short-range forecasting and wind-energy siting, yet sparse radiosonde coverage forces practitioners to interpolate them from a handful of physical predictors. We benchmark modern tabular learners against analytical parameterizations on 158,097 IGRA soundings. CatBoost, TabM, and FT-Transformer reduce RMSE to 1.3-1.6 m/s, against approximately 3 m/s for power-law and Monin-Obukhov fits; once the predictor set is fixed the three architectures differ by less than 0.05 m/s, so accuracy is driven by predictors rather than architecture. A cohort analysis of within-bin profile dispersion places an empirical floor of approximately 1.77 m/s on any point-wise predictor that uses standard radiosonde features, consistent with prior eddy-viscosity inversions. A one-dimensional Fourier Neural Operator applied as a post-hoc corrector to frozen tabular predictions reduces near-surface RMSE on U.S. stations from 1.5 to 1.2 m/s, while leaving upper-layer error unchanged. Further gains should come from new predictors rather than larger models.

papers.title: Computational Power of Clifford and Ising Quantum Computers
papers.abstract: We extend the efficient classical simulation of Ising quantum computers from braidings to measurements. We investigate several different definitions of efficient Clifford quantum computation by varying the power of the circuit generator. In case the circuit generator can see the entire input, we give a detailed proof that efficient simulation of classical computation would imply the separation of complexity classes $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{PSPACE}$. If the circuit generator sees only the input length, we prove that Clifford quantum computers decide what we call affine languages.

papers.title: VC-Dimension and Generalization in Geometric Machine Learning with Applications to Active Learning
papers.abstract: We compute the VC-dimension of metric ball classifiers in the model spaces of Riemannian geometry (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) and present upper and lower bounds on the VC-dimension of metric balls in several other situations, including general normed vector spaces (potentially infinite VC-dimension), vector spaces with $\ell^p$-norms (VC-dimension grows at least linearly in the dimension, faster than Euclidean for $p=1$), flat tori, and general Riemannian manifolds (arbitrarily large VC-dimension after a conformal change). In several situations where the VC-dimension is large or even infinite, we prove generalization bounds under additional assumptions on the data distribution using covering arguments. Both in the VC-dimension and covering setting, we consider data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. As an application, we consider coverage-based algorithms in active learning.

papers.title: Causal mediation analysis for a time-to-event endpoint in the presence of competing events
papers.abstract: Causal mediation analysis is widely used to decompose a treatment's effect into components operating through distinct causal pathways and to characterize the mediator--outcome relationship. In time-to-event settings, competing events --- events that preclude the primary endpoint --- substantially complicate this decomposition. We provide a unified treatment of causal mediation analysis for a time-to-event endpoint under competing events. We show that the total effect on the cause-specific cumulative incidence decomposes into a direct effect, an indirect effect through the mediator of interest, and an indirect effect through the competing events. We develop this decomposition under the natural effects, stochastic interventional effects, and separable effects frameworks, and show that, in certain settings, all three yield identical statistical functionals despite relying on distinct identification assumptions. We derive efficient influence functions for the counterfactual cumulative incidence curves and the decomposed effects, and propose double-machine-learning-type estimators that are multiply robust and attain the semiparametric efficiency bound, with a sensitivity analysis to address unmeasured common causes of time-to-event endpoints. We further study the mediator--outcome response relationship via kernel-smoothed estimands. We apply the methods to immune correlates analyses of COVID-19 vaccine and HIV-1 prevention trials.

papers.title: Early State Exclusion for $5\times5$ Jacobi Matrices
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a problem that arose from quantum computing, when the quantum state to be transferred completely vanishes before the first occurrence of the perfect state transfer. It was posed as an open problem for 1D quantum chains with $n$ of qubits, where $n>4$ is an odd number. We present the solution for $n=5$. The proofs are accessible to students who studied trigonometry and calculus. As for the set-up the knowledge of eigentheory and inner products from linear algebra is needed.

papers.title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

papers.title: XAI-Driven Confidence Estimation for OOD-Resilient Runtime Prediction
papers.abstract: Machine learning-based resource management (RM) models degrade under out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs at runtime, yet existing approaches in the literature rely on a single global error margin that is overly conservative and fails to distinguish reliablepredictions from catastrophic failures. We propose Lightweight Runtime EXplainability (LEX), the first post-hoc XAI framework for input-specific runtime confidence estimation in ML-based RM. LEX clusters the embeddings of the training input space using a Gaussian Mixture Model and associates per-cluster prediction error bounds to input samples, enabling fine-grained runtime confidence signals without retraining. Evaluated on a state-of-the-art LSTM-based IPS forecasting model on Intel Alder Lake, across 34 benchmark applications, LEX achieves ~94% containment on unseen workloads and produces ~17% tighter per-input confidence bounds than global baselines. With its negligible runtime overhead, LEX advances the field by providing explainable and reliable input-specific confidence signals of ML predictions, thereby making ML-based resource management resilient to OOD at runtime.

papers.title: How wide must an eavesdropper be? Leakage of a toric-code logical bit to a strip and the Nishimori point
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers hand pieces of each logical qubit to separate decoder modules and shared readout lines. How much does a piece reveal? We prove that for any region and any Pauli noise, including correlated noise, an observer's optimal advantage in learning a logical bit is exactly 1 - 2 P_fail, where P_fail is the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding confined to that region. Two lessons follow. Geometry, not noise, provides the protection: a region that misses a single column of the code learns exactly nothing at any noise level, while a region that spans the code is protected by noise only at impractical distances (d > 350 for one row at a 10^-3 flip rate). And width is a poor guide to risk: under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip learns exactly as little as one row, yet below threshold an eavesdropper needs a width growing only as ln d. Through the identity, the strip's operational threshold is the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, and a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix up to width 16 locates it to within a few thousandths. On two IBM Heron processors (d = 3, 5), an emulated strip adversary shows the predicted jump at width three, and non-uniform qubit errors let a trained attacker profit from the second row that uniform noise makes useless. We turn these results into design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout. Code and data are included.

papers.title: Rational quantum spectral filtering by repeat-until-success protocol
papers.abstract: We introduce a finite-memory repeat-until-success (RUS) framework for implementing rational spectral filters on a quantum computer, extending spectral filtering beyond the polynomial transformations implemented by quantum signal processing (QSP) and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). Our approach interleaves queries to a block encoding of a Hermitian operator $X$, whose spectrum lies in $[-1,1]$, and mid-circuit measurements that either accept, reject, or continue the computation without resetting the quantum state. Although the protocol may run for arbitrarily many rounds, its terminal statistics are determined by a finite-dimensional Lyapunov equation. Under uniform termination and phase-inversion symmetry, we characterize exactly the spectral filters $R(X)$ realizable upon acceptance: $R$ can be any real rational function with no poles on $[-1,1]$ and values in $[0,1]$. We provide a constructive compiler for any admissible $R$, with bounds on memory and expected query cost, and characterize the accepted quantum operation through a spectral coherence kernel. Applications to regularized resolvents and Lorentzian spectroscopy yield exact low-degree realizations and query-cost advantages over the fixed-depth QSVT polynomial-postselection baseline considered here, with all repetitions and independent restarts after rejection included in the cost.

papers.title: Reconstruction of pion polarizabilities in lattice QCD with machine learning
papers.abstract: We apply the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) from generative machine learning to a model-independent reconstruction of electric and magnetic polarizabilities of both charged and neutral pions. The inputs are the sparse momentum-space four-point-function data in lattice QCD for the connected quark-line contributions obtained in previous simulations at four pion masses between approximately 370 and 1100 MeV on quenched Wilson lattices. For charged pions, the elastic contribution is obtained from the pion form-factor slope, and the complete electric and magnetic inelastic terms are reconstructed separately. The neutral-pion electric and magnetic channels are reconstructed without an elastic charge-radius contribution. Four distinct families of synthetic training functions are employed, so that no single analytic fitting function is prescribed for the lattice data. We present low-momentum reconstructions to the limit of zero momentum transfer where the polarizabilities are defined, and mass extrapolations to the physical pion mass of 138 MeV.

papers.title: Which data samples matter when training a quantum model?
papers.abstract: The expressivity, loss landscapes, and generalization behavior of quantum machine learning models have been studied extensively, yet mainly from a model-centric point of view. Little is known about the compatibility of particular quantum models with specific datasets. In this work, we study quantum machine learning models with a data-dependent focus by establishing a quantum-compatible form of the V-usable information. This metric quantifies the information a model can extract from a dataset, enabling a direct, data-centric comparison of different models. We employ this metric to study which data points contribute most significantly to a model's learning process. This enables us to develop an informed preselection strategy for data subsets that can significantly improve the data efficiency of the training pipeline. This work establishes the V-usable information as a powerful diagnostic tool for learning dynamics and a practical route to data-efficient quantum machine learning.

papers.title: Guiding Data Allocation for Robust Subpopulation Generalization
papers.abstract: Machine learning models often achieve high average accuracy in the training data while performing poorly on test data due to subpopulation shift. A common data-centric solution is to enforce balanced subgroup proportions, but full balance can be costly, infeasible, and not always necessary. In this work, we study whether balanced training data is the unique optimal configuration for robust subpopulation generalization. We extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to theoretically characterize the performance landscape across general training subgroup distributions. We show that multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, can perform comparably to the balanced one. We further derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently. These findings suggest that strategically allocating data offers a more flexible and principled path to robust performance than simple balancing. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/subpop-data-allocation.

papers.title: Chiral waveguide model for error-correctable quantum computation
papers.abstract: We develop a first-principles framework connecting microscopic waveguide scattering to quantum error correction and algorithmic performance. For polarization-encoded single photons interacting with an ensemble of two-level atoms in a chiral waveguide, we derive an effective polarization quantum channel by tracing out the frequency degree of freedom. Using this channel as the physical noise model for a rotated planar code, we observe threshold behavior as the number of atoms $N$ and the atom-waveguide coupling strength $Γ$ are varied. An asymptotic analysis of the microscopic scattering model explains the threshold scaling with $NΓ/σ$, where $σ$ is the photon spectral bandwidth. For identical, lossless atoms with symmetric real coupling and a photon spectrum centered at resonance, the effective noise is strongly biased toward $X$ errors. We then incorporate the resulting logical errors into quantum phase estimation and demonstrate that the noise bias can guide circuit design. In particular, a Hadamard-basis implementation reduces sensitivity to the dominant error, improving algorithmic performance.

papers.title: The simulability frontiers of photonic quantum computing
papers.abstract: Estimates of when photonic devices outgrow classical simulation are hard to compare: even for single-photon boson sampling, quoted thresholds range from 50 to 98 photons, as they rest on different tasks and assumptions. We propose as a common unit the time a classical computer needs to draw one sample from the device's exact output distribution, up to floating-point rounding. Only exactness applies equally to every kind of light, since the cost of approximate sampling depends on the accuracy required. The simulability frontier is the device size at which our fastest exact sampler produces one sample per second on a fixed machine; this device size increases with better hardware and algorithms. As the time per sample grows exponentially with the number of detected photons, doubling the machine speed moves the frontier by about one photon, whereas a better algorithm changes the growth rate. We measure the frontier with photonic-engines, an open-source GPU library of exact samplers for single photons, entangled photons from quantum emitters, vacuum-single-photon superpositions and squeezed light. Each sampler is validated against a simulator sharing no code with it. On one NVIDIA H100 GPU, with Haar-random interferometers, twice as many modes as photonic inputs and photon-number-resolving detectors, the frontier lies at 38.3 single photons and at 31.0 entangled photons from one emitter. For squeezed light, a timing model fitted to measurements places it at 41.5 squeezed photonic inputs of mean photon number 0.5. For our samplers, coherence alone makes simulation harder: sources that emit a photon with probability one half reach 64.2 when vacuum and photon are mixed incoherently, as for lossy single photons, but only 50.0 when they are in coherent superposition. Feed-forward from mid-circuit measurement of up to three modes lowers the single-photon frontier only from 38.3 to 38.1.

papers.title: Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) is a critical for trustworthy machine learning and scientific discovery. Existing methods typically define anomalies through local density, isolation heuristics, or distance from a fitted distribution, making them sensitive to neighborhood scale, partitioning choices, or restrictive distributional assumptions. In this work, we introduce a new paradigm by formulating anomaly detection from a diversity perspective. We propose the $\textit{Vendi Anomaly Score}$ (VAS), which detects anomalies by quantifying how much a sample changes the diversity of the dataset, as measured by the Vendi score, when removed. VAS captures both local redundancy and global data structure without relying on density estimation or partitioning heuristics. Moreover, VAS requires no hyperparameter tuning, instead adapting automatically to the spectral structure of the data. VAS is non-parametric and scales linearly with dataset size. Across 148 benchmark embedding datasets derived from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, VAS achieves state-of-the-art AD performance. We further validate VAS on large-scale ImageNet experiments, where it remains robust as both contamination rate and dataset scale increase.

papers.title: Property F implies weak integrality for non-degenerate pivotal braided fusion categories
papers.abstract: We prove that every non-degenerate pivotal braided fusion category with property F is pseudo-unitary and weakly integral. In particular, every modular category with property F is weakly integral. Neither sphericality nor pseudo-unitarity is assumed. Passing to the Drinfeld centre extends the result to degenerate categories whose dimensions are positive on the intersection of the Müger centre with the adjoint subcategory; these include every braided fusion category with a pseudo-unitary Galois conjugate. Physically, the result connects the arithmetic of topological orders to the computational power of anyon braiding: non-integer squared total quantum dimension guarantees infinite braid group images, a necessary condition for universal quantum computation.

papers.title: Automated Knowledge Acquisition Pipeline for Disassembly Instructions: A Comparison of NLP and Generative AI Frameworks
papers.abstract: The push towards circularity and Re-X principles presents a challenge to SMEs, particularly due to increasing product complexity that impedes the adoption of disassembly automation. This paper introduces and compares two frameworks for extracting disassembly instructions from unstructured information sources, such as disassembly manuals. Our goal is to transform natural language text into a structured, curated and machine-readable format. We implemented and tested a rule-based Natural Language Processing (NLP) framework against a generative AI framework leveraging LLMs. The performance of both approaches was compared using real-world disassembly manuals. This work provides the necessary data foundation for developing and automating future disassembly processes.

papers.title: The Radicalization Pipeline: Characterizing and Predicting Online Misogyny
papers.abstract: Social media platforms are known to shape and polarize user opinions and, increasingly, facilitate pathways toward ideological extremism. Among these trends, online misogynistic communities associ- ated with the incel (involuntary celibate) ideology have received growing scholarly attention. Previous work has primarily focused on ideological narratives and linguistic content within incel communities them- selves. However, much less is known about how user behaviors evolve over time, particularly before and after their engagement with incel spaces, and whether early signals can anticipate such transitions. In this study, we conduct a longitudinal analysis of Reddit users who participated in the r/incels community on Reddit. Our results show that engagement with the incel community is associated with a substantial in- crease in toxicity in both posts and comments, while hate increases particularly in posts after engagement. These changes extend beyond explicitly ideological communities: users who engage with the r/incels sub- reddit display elevated toxicity and hate speech even in subreddits related to leisure, entertainment, and everyday interests. In parallel, user activity shifts away from recreational and support-oriented communi- ties toward subreddits focused on social issues, indicating a broader reorientation of online participation. Finally, we show that future incel users can be identified with high accuracy prior to engagement using supervised machine learning models trained on linguistic, contextual, and interaction-based features. These findings suggest that online misogynistic radicalization follows detectable behavioral trajectories and diffuses across the broader social media ecosystem.

papers.title: Large Language Models as a Universal Searcher for Open-World Automated Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Developing effective machine learning models requires complex manual tuning, while current Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) frameworks remain domain-specific and isolate model architecture, training hyperparameter, and data ratio optimization. Here, we bridge this gap by proposing a universal, large language model (LLM)-based AutoML framework that jointly optimizes these configurations for the first time without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. We propose NCode, a unified numerical encoding scheme that translates diverse AutoML design choices into universal discrete sequences and effectively reframes the optimization process as a unified ranking task. Trained solely on optimization trajectories derived from a limited, single-domain vision task, the proposed LLM-based searcher demonstrates impressive cross-task, cross-modality and joint search-space optimization generalizability, achieving state-of-the-art performance across image classification, image segmentation, speaker verification and text-to-image benchmarks. Crucially, it exhibits superior scalability in the large-scale training and joint optimization of a billion-parameter Diffusion Transformer, requiring 896 GPU-days and attaining a state-of-the-art GenEval score of 0.91. By leveraging reinforcement learning to instill Chain-of-Thought reasoning, we provide a systematic way to interpret the LLM-based searcher's internal decision-making mechanisms, revealing its optimization strategy shifted from the early-stage diversity-driven exploration to the late-stage anchor exploitation. Our proposed framework provides a scalable, generalizable, and interpretable pathway toward general-purpose open-world machine learning optimization.

papers.title: MarsNet: Learning the Martian Atmosphere from Observations Alone
papers.abstract: We present MarsNet, a machine-learned model of the Martian atmosphere trained only on observations. Existing reanalyses assimilate spacecraft retrievals into general circulation models (GCMs), so where observations are sparse their fields largely reflect the model. We therefore use extant reanalyses only for evaluation. MarsNet alternates a two-hour forecast with an update that assimilates the observations of each window, and both steps are learned jointly. Because the Martian record is too sparse for an unrestricted network, learning is confined within a fixed physical structure: the state is in physical units, the forecast uses physical tendencies of fixed form and learned strength, and the update is a bounded Kalman update. MarsNet is trained on Mars Years (MY) 24--31 and evaluated on independent observations. On three seasons of MGS radio-occultation temperatures assimilated by no dataset, MarsNet matches or improves on the three reanalyses in the lowest three scale heights, with a near-surface root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 4.2 K against 4.4--5.4 K, but is less accurate aloft. The model's surface pressures are the most accurate of the four products (RMSE 10 Pa against Curiosity in MY32, compared with 20--46 Pa). On withheld Mars Climate Sounder profiles of MY32, its temperatures beat an observed climatology and persistence, including in ten-sol forecasts without new observations, and its stated uncertainty is close to calibrated. Much of the temperature skill is present before training and appears to come from the structure and tables fitted to the observations, while training mainly improves the surface pressures, at some cost to dust. The model cycles stably through nine Mars years, and the influence of each observation can be traced. Its speed makes experiments on the observing record practical, and it offers an independent reference for GCMs and reanalyses.

papers.title: Quantum Simulation of Quantum Channels and Applications
papers.abstract: We review the basic theory of quantum channels and develop a strategy for simulating them on digital quantum computers, drawing upon the Choi-Kraus operator-sum representation and Stinespring dilation to provide a unified approach for various applications. We discuss three types of applications, offering explicit examples for each: the preparation of mixed states, measurements described by positive operator-valued measures (POVMs), and the simulation of the evolution of Markovian quantum systems. We recover fundamental concepts from quantum theory, such as the purification of a mixed state and the Naimark dilation associated with a POVM. Regarding the simulation of the evolution of a Markovian quantum system, we introduce an operator, termed the residual operator, to construct, from the system's Liouvillian, a quantum channel that serves as a first-order approximation of the quantum dynamical semigroup. This allows the simulation of quantum dynamics to be performed in a manner analogous to the Euler method for ordinary differential equations, avoiding Trotterization. We prove all the theoretical results mentioned, with the exception of the fundamental Choi-Kraus theorem concerning the operator-sum representation of quantum channels, for which we provide the appropriate references. The explicit simulations discussed were implemented using the AerSimulator from IBM's Qiskit SDK, with the corresponding code available on GitHub.

papers.title: $\mathsf{EQP}\subseteq\mathsf{IP}$ Does Not Relativize
papers.abstract: We construct a recursive oracle $O$ and a unary language $L\in\mathsf{EQP}^O\setminus(\mathsf{IP}^O\cup\mathsf{PH}^O)$, strengthening the $\mathsf{BQP}$ versus $\mathsf{IP}$ oracle separation of Bouland et al. to exact quantum computation. The separation is based on a variant of the Forrelation problem in which the normalized correlation of one Boolean function with the Fourier transform of another is promised to be exactly $+1/2$ or $-1/2$. The main technical contribution is a repair method that constructs distributions supported on these exact levels while preserving the indistinguishability needed for the $\mathsf{IP}$ and $\mathsf{PH}$ lower bounds. A uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm distinguishes the two cases with certainty using only three oracle queries.

papers.title: Finite temperature and pressure structural relaxations including zero-point motion and anharmonicity
